results.name: odd_set_odd_target_yes
results.description: Yes rate for odd targets (not themselves examples) when all examples are odd and there are >=2 of them; observed below the null means the model over-produces "odd numbers" generalization (gives the parity rule too much weight), above means it under-produces it.
results.code:
# name: odd_set_odd_target_yes
# description: Yes rate for odd targets (not themselves examples) when all examples are odd and there are >=2 of them; observed below the null means the model over-produces "odd numbers" generalization (gives the parity rule too much weight), above means it under-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    allodd = np.all(~valid | (np.nan_to_num(ex) % 2 == 1), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = allodd & (n >= 2) & (t % 2 == 1) & ~inset
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: tens_vs_units_digit_match
results.description: Among non-example targets 10-99 in sets with any two-digit example, yes rate for targets whose tens digit equals some example's tens digit (and units matches none) minus yes rate for targets whose units digit equals some example's units digit (and tens matches none); observed above the null means the model under-weights decade (tens-position) similarity relative to last-digit similarity, below means the reverse.
results.code:
# name: tens_vs_units_digit_match
# description: Among non-example targets 10-99 in sets with any two-digit example, yes rate for targets whose tens digit equals some example's tens digit (and units matches none) minus yes rate for targets whose units digit equals some example's units digit (and tens matches none); observed above the null means the model under-weights decade (tens-position) similarity relative to last-digit similarity, below means the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    two = (ex >= 10) & (ex <= 99)
    et = np.where(two, np.floor(np.nan_to_num(ex) / 10), -1)
    eu = np.where(two, np.nan_to_num(ex) % 10, -1)
    tt = (t // 10)[:, None]; tu = (t % 10)[:, None]
    tm = np.any(et == tt, axis=1); um = np.any(eu == tu, axis=1)
    inset = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (t >= 10) & (t <= 99) & ~inset & two.any(axis=1)
    a = y[base & tm & ~um]; b = y[base & um & ~tm]
    return float((a.mean() if a.size else 0.0) - (b.mean() if b.size else 0.0))

results.name: interior_nondigit_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the examples' range (min<t<max, multi-example sets, range>=10) that share no digit with any example and are not examples; observed above the null means the model under-produces interval (magnitude) generalization when a digit rule competes, below means it over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: interior_nondigit_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets strictly inside the examples' range (min<t<max, multi-example sets, range>=10) that share no digit with any example and are not examples; observed above the null means the model under-produces interval (magnitude) generalization when a digit rule competes, below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    td = np.array([[str(v).count(str(d)) > 0 for d in range(10)] for v in range(101)])
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0).astype(int)
    exd = np.zeros((len(df), 10), bool)
    for j in range(ex.shape[1]):
        exd |= td[exi[:, j]] & ~np.isnan(ex[:, j])[:, None]
    share = np.any(exd & td[t], axis=1)
    inset = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (hi - lo >= 10) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~share & ~inset
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: adjacent_to_example_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets exactly 1 or 2 away from some example (not themselves examples), all sets; observed above the null means the model under-produces near-neighbour (numerical similarity) generalization, below means it over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: adjacent_to_example_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets exactly 1 or 2 away from some example (not themselves examples), all sets; observed above the null means the model under-produces near-neighbour (numerical similarity) generalization, below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 2)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: strong_units_rule_nonmember_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets whose last digit differs from the shared last digit of a >=3-example set whose examples all end in the same digit; observed below the null means the model (via lapse guessing and intervals) over-produces "yes" to clear rule violators, above means humans accept violators more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: strong_units_rule_nonmember_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets whose last digit differs from the shared last digit of a >=3-example set whose examples all end in the same digit; observed below the null means the model (via lapse guessing and intervals) over-produces "yes" to clear rule violators, above means humans accept violators more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    u = np.where(valid, np.nan_to_num(ex) % 10, np.nan)
    u0 = u[:, 0]
    same = np.all(~valid | (u == u0[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = same & (n >= 3) & (t % 10 != u0)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: above_minus_below_range_yes
results.description: Yes rate for non-digit-sharing targets 1-20 above the example maximum minus that for targets 1-20 below the example minimum; observed differing from the null means the model's symmetric intervals miss a directional (upward vs downward) extension bias, positive = humans extend upward more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_range_yes
# description: Yes rate for non-digit-sharing targets 1-20 above the example maximum minus that for targets 1-20 below the example minimum; observed differing from the null means the model's symmetric intervals miss a directional (upward vs downward) extension bias, positive = humans extend upward more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    td = np.array([[str(d) in str(v) for d in range(10)] for v in range(101)])
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0).astype(int)
    exd = np.zeros((len(df), 10), bool)
    for j in range(ex.shape[1]):
        exd |= td[exi[:, j]] & ~np.isnan(ex[:, j])[:, None]
    share = np.any(exd & td[t], axis=1)
    up = (t > hi) & (t <= hi + 20) & ~share
    dn = (t < lo) & (t >= lo - 20) & ~share
    a = y[up].mean() if up.any() else 0.0
    b = y[dn].mean() if dn.any() else 0.0
    return float(a - b)

results.name: single_example_shared_digit_contrast
results.description: For one-example sets (target != example), yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the example minus yes rate for targets sharing none; observed above the null means the model under-produces digit-based generalization from a single example (equal prior underweights digit rules), below means it over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: single_example_shared_digit_contrast
# description: For one-example sets (target != example), yes rate for targets sharing a digit with the example minus yes rate for targets sharing none; observed above the null means the model under-produces digit-based generalization from a single example (equal prior underweights digit rules), below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0")).astype(int).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    td = np.array([[str(d) in str(v) for d in range(10)] for v in range(101)])
    share = np.any(td[x] & td[t], axis=1)
    m = single.to_numpy() & (t != x)
    a = y[m & share]; b = y[m & ~share]
    return float((a.mean() if a.size else 0.0) - (b.mean() if b.size else 0.0))

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: In multi-example sets, yes rate for targets within 5 of the last-shown example (but not within 5 of the first) minus that for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (but not the last), excluding examples; the model is order-invariant, so observed above the null means humans weight the most recent example more (recency), below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: In multi-example sets, yes rate for targets within 5 of the last-shown example (but not within 5 of the first) minus that for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (but not the last), excluding examples; the model is order-invariant, so observed above the null means humans weight the most recent example more (recency), below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(df)), n - 1]
    inset = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    nf = np.abs(t - first) <= 5; nl = np.abs(t - last) <= 5
    base = (n >= 2) & ~inset
    a = y[base & nl & ~nf]; b = y[base & nf & ~nl]
    return float((a.mean() if a.size else 0.0) - (b.mean() if b.size else 0.0))
